citation: Slazus BJ, Bick G (2022). Factors that influence FinTech adoption in South Africa: a study of consumer behaviour towards branchless mobile banking. Athens Journal of Business & Economics 8(1): 43-64 (qualitative interview phase).

claims.text: Familiarity is the bridge: a new channel is adopted when it reads as an extension of what the user already does, not as a novel risk
evaluative_rules: Judge a new channel by whether it extends what you already use, not by its novelty
objections: Does this fit with what I already do, or is it a whole new risk?

readings.text: Someone who sees a new channel as an extension of what they already do on their PC would weigh a new product by how closely it mirrors the steps they already know from internet banking.

If a new service is framed as an extension of internet banking, someone who already uses internet banking would assess it primarily for continuity with their existing PC habits rather than as a separate risk.
Someone who adopted m-banking because it extended their internet banking would be less open to a new product that requires learning a different routine from the one they already use on their PC.

If a new product is presented as a novel risk rather than an extension of what they already do, someone who values familiarity would weigh it with more caution than a product that connects to their existing internet banking.

claims.text: Convenience is the pull: always-available access from a device already in hand makes the channel worth using
evaluative_rules: Weigh a channel by convenience and round-the-clock access
objections: Can I get to it whenever I need it, from what I already carry?

readings.text: Someone who values always-available access from a device already in hand would weigh a new service mainly by whether it removes steps they currently take elsewhere.
If convenience is the pull, a new product that adds even a small amount of setup or waiting would feel less worth using than the channel they already reach for.
Someone who sees the channel as worth using because it is always available would be more open to a new offering only when it works on the phone or iPad they already carry.
If the device in hand is what makes the channel worth using, a new policy that requires a different device or a separate visit would be weighed as a loss of that convenience.

claims.text: Security measures such as fingerprint login make the app feel comfortable, so it is read as a secure and trustworthy place to bank.
evaluative_rules: Judge a channel by whether its security feels easy and reassuring, not burdensome
objections: Does it make me feel safe without making me work for it?

readings.text: Someone who feels comfortable because security measures are in place would weigh a new banking feature by first checking whether it preserves that sense of protection.
If fingerprint login makes the app feel comfortable and secure, a new service that adds extra steps before access would be seen as undermining that ease.
Someone who finds fingerprint authentication easier and quicker than a password would be more open to a new policy that keeps biometric login as the default.
If the app is read as a secure and trustworthy place to bank because of fingerprint login, a new product that works only on devices without biometrics would be treated with caution.

claims.text: Traditional banking feels more expensive, so a cheaper channel is a reason to switch.
evaluative_rules: Weigh a channel by whether it costs less than the traditional way
objections: Is it actually cheaper than what I use now?

readings.text: Someone who switched because m-banking was cheaper would weigh a new service mainly on whether it keeps things below traditional banking.
Someone who found the app cheaper would be less open to a new service if it does not clearly show it is cheaper than traditional banking.
If the new service is cheaper only in some situations, this person would weigh it against the app they already use for lower prices.
Someone who already switched for a cheaper channel would still consider a new service if it is presented as cheaper than traditional banking.

claims.text: Human contact is the trust anchor: a fully digitised experience without a person to speak to is read as untrustworthy and incomplete
evaluative_rules: Judge a channel by whether you can still reach a human when you need one
objections: Can I speak to a human if something goes wrong?

readings.text: If a new service is fully digitised, they would weigh it as untrustworthy and incomplete unless it offers a way to speak to a human.
Someone who wants to be able to speak to a human would weigh a new service more favourably if it includes a person to speak to as part of the experience.
If a new service is completely digitised, they would weigh it as incomplete even if it is efficient, because it lacks the human contact they use as a trust anchor.
Someone who does not trust a completely digitised experience would weigh a new service with human contact as more trustworthy than one without it.

confidence: Seven in-depth interviews with South African bank customers about mobile banking (the qualitative phase of a mixed-methods study). Thin: few voices, demographics not reported. Mechanisms plausible; magnitudes unknown.
subject: banking, mobile money and digital payments: trusting a bank, wallet or payment app to hold or move your money
year_note: Published 2022; the qualitative phase is 7 in-depth interviews before a survey, which is not used here.
